qs.q: An unvaccinated adult presents with fever, malaise, and a maculopapular rash that began on the face and spread downward, accompanied by post-auricular lymphadenopathy. What is the virus?
o: Measles virus belonging to the Morbillivirus genus
Rubella virus belonging to the Togaviridae family
Parvovirus B19 causing classical slapped cheeks
Human herpesvirus 6 inducing roseola infantum
Varicella-zoster virus forming vesicular crops
qs.e: Rubella virus causes German measles, characterized by descending rash and prominent post-auricular lymphadenopathy.

qs.q: A 10-year-old child has pharyngitis and cervical lymphadenopathy. Lab confirms infectious mononucleosis. Which viral family is the causative agent?
o: Reoviridae family containing a double-stranded RNA genome
Picornaviridae family containing a single-stranded RNA genome
Rhabdoviridae family containing a single-stranded RNA genome
Herpesviridae family containing a double-stranded DNA genome
Togaviridae family containing a single-stranded RNA genome
qs.e: Epstein-Barr Virus, which causes infectious mononucleosis, belongs to the Herpesviridae family.

qs.q: A 19-year-old college student presents with fever, sore throat, and generalized lymphadenopathy. Peripheral blood film shows atypical lymphocytes. Serology is positive for heterophile antibodies. Which host cell is the primary target of the etiologic agent?
o: Helper T lymphocytes via CD4 molecules
Cytotoxic T lymphocytes via CD8 markers
Memory B lymphocytes via CD21 receptors
Follicular dendritic cells in lymph nodes
Endothelial cells lining postcapillary venules
qs.e: Epstein-Barr virus infects B cells by binding to the CD21 complement receptor, stimulating polyclonal antibody production.

qs.q: A 5-year-old child presents with high fever, pharyngitis, conjunctivitis, and cervical lymphadenopathy after swimming in a public pool. Which structural characteristic allows the causative pathogen to survive harsh environmental conditions in water?
o: Heat-shock protein incorporation stabilizes the viral attachment spike
A thick outer peptidoglycan layer protects the viral core from lysis
Absence of a lipid envelope renders the capsid resistant to chlorine
Covalent cross-linking of structural proteins prevents desiccation
A double-layered outer protein shell buffers against pH fluctuations
qs.e: Adenoviruses lack a lipid envelope, making them non-enveloped and resistant to common disinfectants like chlorine.

qs.q: A 35-year-old woman presents with a persistent cough and shortness of breath. On chest X-ray, bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy is seen. What is the most likely diagnosis?
o: Consistent with primary lung cancer
Consistent with systemic lymphoma
Consistent with pulmonary tuberculosis
Consistent with pulmonary sarcoidosis
Consistent with bacterial pneumonia
qs.e: Bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy is a classic radiographic finding in sarcoidosis, a systemic granulomatous disease.

qs.q: A 6-year-old child presents with persistent fever for 8 days, bilateral non-exudative conjunctivitis, polymorphous rash, erythematous changes of the oral mucosa and palms, and cervical lymphadenopathy. What is the most critical long-term complication that dictates early therapeutic intervention?
o: Develop chronic obstructive pulmonary disease and fibrosis.
Develop aseptic meningitis and hydrocephalus.
Develop progressive glomerulosclerosis and renal failure.
Develop coronary artery aneurysms and ectasia.
Develop permanent osteonecrosis of the femoral head.
qs.e: Kawasaki disease requires early treatment with intravenous immunoglobulin to prevent coronary artery aneurysms.

qs.q: A patient presents with a painless, indurated genital ulcer accompanied by regional lymphadenopathy. Darkfield microscopy of scrapings reveals highly motile, slender spiral bacteria. What is the primary virulence strategy that accounts for the relative paucity of surface proteins on this organism?
o: Possession of a remarkably sparse outer membrane protein
Rapid antigenic variation driven by frequent gene conversion
Complete shedding of its outer sheath upon host recognition
Sequestration inside host cell lysosomes to hide antigens
Production of thick capsules that mask all membrane proteins
qs.e: Treponema pallidum features an unusually sparse outer membrane protein content, which helps it evade recognition by the host immune system.

qs.q: A 5-year-old child presents with high fever, pharyngitis, conjunctivitis, and tender preauricular lymphadenopathy after swimming in a public pool. Which structural characteristic allows the causative agent to survive harsh environmental conditions in water?
o: Lack of a lipid envelope makes the capsid resistant to detergents and drying.
A thick outer protein coat containing peptidoglycan remnants provides protection.
Cross‑linked penton base proteins form a covalent barrier against aqueous solvents.
A dense tegument layer shields the double‑stranded DNA genome from osmotic lysis.
An outer polysaccharide capsule prevents water influx in hypotonic solutions.
qs.e: Adenoviruses are non-enveloped DNA viruses, lacking a lipid bilayer, which makes them stable in water and resistant to chlorine.

es.q: A 55-year-old patient of Chinese descent presents with cervical lymphadenopathy. Biopsy reveals an undifferentiated carcinoma of the nasopharynx. Discuss the primary etiological agent strongly linked to this condition and describe the characteristic histological features of the undifferentiated vari
es.m: Nasopharyngeal carcinoma is strongly linked to the Epstein-Barr Virus (EBV), with the viral genome found in virtually all cases, particularly in high-incidence Chinese populations. EBV first replicates in nasopharyngeal epithelium before infecting tonsillar B lymphocytes, leading to epithelial transformation. The undifferentiated carcinoma variant, which is the most common and most closely linked to EBV, is characterized histologically by large epithelial cells with indistinct cell borders, often described as having a "syncytial" growth pattern. These cells also feature prominent eosinophilic nucleoli. The tumor typically grows against a background of prominent reactive lymphocytes, which ca

es.q: A 68-year-old male presents with new-onset, painless cervical lymphadenopathy. Biopsy confirms Non-Hodgkin Lymphoma (NHL). Briefly outline the primary cellular origins of NHL and their approximate percentages.
es.m: Non-Hodgkin Lymphoma is a diverse group of clonal lymphoid tumors. Approximately 85% are of B-cell origin, while 15% arise from T or NK cells.

es.q: A 58-year-old patient presents with several months of unexplained fever, night sweats, and significant weight loss, alongside generalized, painless lymphadenopathy. es.m: Non-Hodgkin Lymphoma (NHL) represents a diverse group of clonal lymphoid tumors. It is the fifth most common malignancy in developed countries, with a rising incidence over the last 50 years. es.s: Non-Hodgkin Lymphoma: Classification, Symptoms, Diagnosis, and Treatment — Pract

es.q: A 55-year-old patient of Chinese descent presents with cervical lymphadenopathy. Biopsy reveals an undifferentiated carcinoma of the nasopharynx. Discuss the etiology and key histological features of this specific variant.

ai.clinicalScope: Lymphadenopathy in children and adults presenting to low‑resource East African hospitals, focusing on common infectious, inflammatory and malignant causes
ai.title: Lymphadenopathy
ai.subject: Pathology
ai.summary: Lymphadenopathy means enlarged lymph nodes. It can be caused by infections, immune diseases, or cancer, and the pattern of enlargement helps doctors decide what to investigate and treat.

sections.p: Lymphadenopathy is palpable enlargement of one or more lymph nodes. Classification is based on size, number, location, duration and tenderness.
b: Size thresholds: cervical >1 cm (or >0.5 cm if tender), axillary >0.5 cm, inguinal >1 cm
Localized (single region) vs generalized (≥2 non‑contiguous regions)
Acute (<2 weeks) vs chronic (>2 weeks)
Tender (often infectious) vs non‑tender (often malignant or granulomatous)
Hard, fixed nodes raise suspicion for malignancy; soft, mobile nodes are usually benign

sections.p: In low‑resource East Africa the most frequent causes are infectious, followed by autoimmune and neoplastic conditions.
b: Tuberculosis (TB) – cervical or supraclavicular, matted, often with constitutional symptoms
HIV‑associated opportunistic infections (TB, cryptococcosis, Kaposi sarcoma)
Malaria or acute bacterial skin infections – tender, regional nodes
Schistosomiasis – peri‑portal lymphadenopathy
Rheumatic diseases (e.g., systemic lupus erythematosus) – generalized, non‑tender
Hodgkin and non‑Hodgkin lymphoma – firm, non‑tender, often cervical or mediastinal
Metastatic carcinoma (e.g., breast, head‑neck) – hard, fixed nodes
Drug reactions (e.g., antitubercular therapy, sulfonamides) – generalized, often with rash

sections.p: Enlargement results from increased cellularity, fluid, or fibrosis within the node.
b: Infection → antigen presentation → proliferation of lymphocytes and macrophages → node swelling
Granulomatous disease (TB, sarcoidosis) → caseating or non‑caseating granulomas → fibrosis and persistent enlargement
Malignancy → clonal proliferation of neoplastic cells → replacement of normal architecture
Obstruction of lymphatic drainage (e.g., tumour encasement) → edema and node distension

sections.p: Visible changes guide the next diagnostic step.
b: Tender, fluctuant nodes may indicate abscess formation
Matted, rubbery nodes suggest TB or fungal infection
Hard, irregular, fixed nodes raise suspicion for lymphoma or metastatic cancer
Red, warm overlying skin points to cellulitis or suppurative infection

sections.p: Histology differentiates infectious, granulomatous, and neoplastic processes.
b: Acute suppurative lymphadenitis – neutrophilic infiltrate, necrosis
TB lymphadenitis – caseating granulomas with Langhans giant cells
Sarcoidosis – non‑caseating epithelioid granulomas, minimal necrosis
Hodgkin lymphoma – Reed‑Sternberg cells in a mixed inflammatory background
Non‑Hodgkin lymphoma – diffuse sheets of atypical lymphocytes

sections.p: Symptoms and signs vary with cause and node location.
b: Fever, night sweats, weight loss – classic ‘B‑symptoms’ of TB or lymphoma
Localized pain, erythema – acute bacterial lymphadenitis
Pruritus or skin rash – drug reaction or HIV‑related disease
Dyspnoea or cough with mediastinal nodes – sarcoidosis or TB
Upper‑limb swelling if axillary nodes obstruct venous return

sections.p: Choose tests that answer the clinical question; adapt when resources are limited.

t.b: Is the node malignant or granulomatous? – Cytology showing malignant cells or granulomas guides further management
What is the definitive histology? – Gold standard for lymphoma, sarcoidosis, TB when FNAC is inconclusive
Is there hilar or mediastinal lymphadenopathy? – Bilateral hilar nodes suggest sarcoidosis; unilateral may be TB

t.a: GeneXpert MTB/RIF on node tissue or aspirate
t.b: Is Mycobacterium tuberculosis present? – Positive result confirms TB; negative does not exclude paucibacillary disease
Is immunosuppression a factor? – Positive test prompts evaluation for opportunistic infections and lymphoma
Are there systemic inflammatory markers? – Elevated ESR/CRP supports infection or inflammation; anemia may suggest chronic disease
Is there a cystic/necrotic centre? – Suggests abscess; preserved hilum favours reactive hyperplasia

sections.p: Staging helps decide treatment intensity, especially for lymphoma.
b: Stage I – single nodal region, ≤1.5 cm, no systemic symptoms
Stage II – multiple nodes in one region, ≤2 cm, mild B‑symptoms
Stage III – nodes >2 cm, marked B‑symptoms, or involvement of extranodal sites
For TB, WHO defines ‘simple lymphadenitis’ (single node, <3 cm) vs ‘complex’ (multiple, matted, >3 cm, or with sinus formation)

sections.p: Complications depend on underlying cause and timeliness of treatment.
b: Node rupture → sinus tract formation, chronic discharge (TB)
Compression of adjacent structures – airway obstruction (mediastinal nodes), vascular compromise
Progression to disseminated disease – miliary TB, metastatic cancer
Lymphoma – risk of marrow infiltration, CNS involvement
In HIV, untreated lymphadenopathy may herald opportunistic infection or lymphoma with poor prognosis

sections.p: Treat the underlying cause; provide supportive care and monitor response.
b: TB lymphadenitis – 6‑month rifampicin‑based regimen; surgical excision only for large sinuses or diagnostic uncertainty
Acute bacterial lymphadenitis – empiric amoxicillin/clavulanate (or cloxacillin) for 7‑10 days; incision and drainage if fluctuant
Hodgkin lymphoma – ABVD chemotherapy (adriamycin, bleomycin, vinblastine, dacarbazine) – dose details omitted; radiotherapy for residual disease
Non‑Hodgkin lymphoma – CHOP regimen or targeted therapy based on subtype
Sarcoidosis – oral prednisone for symptomatic disease; monitor calcium and ACE levels
Supportive measures – analgesia, antipyretics, nutrition, HIV antiretroviral therapy if positive

sections.p: Linking node characteristics to histology improves diagnostic accuracy.
b: Matted, rubbery cervical nodes + night sweats → TB lymphadenitis (caseating granulomas)
Hard, fixed supraclavicular node in a smoker → metastatic lung carcinoma (malignant cells on biopsy)
Bilateral hilar nodes with erythema nodosum → sarcoidosis (non‑caseating granulomas)
Rapidly enlarging, painful node with overlying erythema → suppurative bacterial infection (neutrophils on cytology)

sections.p: A systematic bedside method ensures no key clue is missed.
b: History – onset, duration, pain, constitutional symptoms, recent infections, travel, HIV risk, drug exposures
Inspection – skin changes, drainage, symmetry
Palpation – size, consistency, mobility, tenderness, matting, fluctuation
Systemic exam – lungs, abdomen, skin, neurologic signs for disseminated disease
Prioritize urgent red flags: rapid growth >2 cm in 48 h, fixed hard node, overlying ulceration, severe systemic illness

whenToSeekHelp: Rapidly enlarging node >2 cm within 48 h
Hard, fixed node with weight loss or night sweats
Overlying skin ulceration or abscess formation
Associated high fever (>38.5 °C) and sepsis signs

faq.q: Can a small tender node be serious?
faq.a: Most tender nodes are reactive, but if they persist >2 weeks or are associated with systemic symptoms, further evaluation is needed.

faq.q: Why is excisional biopsy preferred over FNAC for lymphoma?
faq.a: Excisional biopsy provides architecture, essential for lymphoma sub‑typing and staging, which FNAC cannot reliably deliver.

faq.q: What if GeneXpert is negative but TB is still suspected?
faq.a: Repeat testing, obtain a larger tissue sample for histology, or start empirical anti‑TB therapy if clinical suspicion is high.

exam: A 28‑year‑old HIV‑positive man presents with a 3‑cm painless cervical node, night sweats and weight loss – what is the next best investigation and why? — Excisional biopsy to obtain definitive histology for lymphoma or TB, because FNAC may miss architecture.

A child from a malaria‑endemic area has tender axillary nodes and fever – which cause is most likely and what initial management should you start? — Acute bacterial lymphadenitis; start empiric amoxicillin/clavulanate and monitor for abscess formation.
How does the presence of caseating granulomas on node biopsy narrow the differential? — It points toward TB or fungal infection, excluding sarcoidosis which shows non‑caseating granulomas.
Why is a hard, fixed supraclavicular node considered a red flag even in a low‑resource setting? — It suggests metastatic carcinoma or lymphoma, both requiring urgent tissue diagnosis and staging.

In a patient with generalized lymphadenopathy and a positive HIV test, what opportunistic infection should be ruled out first? — Mycobacterial TB, because it is common and can present with matted cervical nodes.

What clinical feature distinguishes sarcoidosis from TB when both cause hilar lymphadenopathy? — Presence of erythema nodosum and hypercalcaemia favours sarcoidosis; cavitary lung lesions and positive sputum smear favour TB.
When is surgical excision of a TB node indicated? — When there is a persistent sinus, large (>3 cm) node not responding to therapy, or diagnostic uncertainty after biopsy.
Explain why a rapid rise in ESR is not specific for lymphoma. — ESR rises in any chronic inflammation, infection, or autoimmune disease, so it must be interpreted with clinical context.
A patient presents with a fluctuant inguinal node after a foot ulcer – what is the likely diagnosis and immediate step? — Suppurative lymphadenitis; perform incision and drainage plus antibiotics.

How would you modify the work‑up if ultrasound is unavailable? — Rely on clinical assessment, FNAC, chest X‑ray, and empirical therapy based on epidemiology; arrange referral for biopsy when possible.
